㊙️内部情報
Seedance 2.0 Mini が明日公開されるみたいです。

① コストを大幅削減
・クレジット消費量は従来の半分（1/2）
・同じ予算でより多くの動画を生成可能

・制作全体の効率を向上

・軽量化による品質低下をできる限り抑制
⑤ より高い安定性
・高速生成と安定した出力を両立
・複数ショットや繰り返し生成時の一貫性が向上
・再生成の手間を減らしやすい

This is wild 

Browser automation as we know it is over

page-agent.js— a GUI agent that runs inside your webpage itself. No Selenium. No Puppeteer. No extensions. No backend. One script tag.

It reads the DOM as plain text (no screenshots, no multimodal models, no special permissions), works with any LLM you bring, and executes plain-English commands like "fill out this form" or "submit the order" — directly in the page.

The use cases are wild:

→ Ship an AI copilot inside your SaaS in literally lines of code
→ Collapse 20-click ERP/CRM workflows into a single sentence
→ Give any legacy web app voice + natural language control
→ Extend it across tabs with the optional Chrome extension, or drive it externally via MCP

12k+ stars. MIT licensed. Built on browser-use internals — with zero setup overhead.

Everyone's been debating what "AI-native UX" means.

title: Inside soccer’s data renaissance
content: Imagine tuning in to the opening kickoff of a World Cup match and seeing a player intentionally send the ball all the way down the pitch and right out of bounds on the opponent’s end. Casual fans might scratch their heads. Where’s the logic in surrendering possession seconds into a game? If you were Jesse Davis, though, you’d know that this play could be a prime setup to score.  Davis is a professor of computer science at KU Leuven in Belgium and head of its Sports Analytics Lab , which has been at the vanguard of a data awakening in soccer since its inception more than a decade ago. Though the research group brings machine-­learning models to bear on a variety of sports—including basketball, volleyball, and field hockey—nowhere is its impact felt more than on the soccer pitch.  Davis and his team of researchers employ advanced data analytics to reveal a range of (beg your pardon) game-changing findings that are shifting pro clubs’ decision-making. “His lab is the most influential sports analytics lab in soccer,” says Hugo Rios-Neto, data recruitment lead for Royal Sporting Club Anderlecht in Belgium. They’ve helped teams better evaluate their rosters, conceived ways to assess how efficient (or not) strategies are, and developed algorithms that uncover hidden tactical patterns. Like, for instance, the value of kicking the ball out of bounds close to the goal and letting your opponent throw it back into play—a move that’s been popping up in some of the world’s top leagues over the last few years. To make the statistical argument for this seemingly counterproductive move, Davis’s group built a training data set composed of more than 1.4 million passes and some 60,000 throw-ins—partly from the 2022 World Cup. They used tree ensemble models (essentially a mashup of decision trees) to simulate the tactic. title: Why China is betting on big nuclear reactors
content: It’s a tale of two nuclear industries. In China, large reactors are coming together at a stunning pace. The country has nearly doubled its nuclear fleet since 2016, reaching nearly 60 gigawatts of total power capacity. The new facilities are nearly all gigawatt-scale pressurized-water reactors. Meanwhile, the US has built just two reactors in that time—Unit 3 and Unit 4 at Plant Vogtle in Georgia. Smaller reactors are attracting a lot of excitement and investment, though. A microreactor developer just saw its reactor reach criticality in a new Department of Energy pilot program. The world is racing to meet rising electricity demand, and many countries are interested in energy sources, like nuclear power, that don’t come with greenhouse-gas emissions. The key question: Which of these strategies will really pay off in terms of getting electrons on the grid quickly?   Today, the US and France are known as leaders in the nuclear industry. The US has the world’s largest fleet, with France coming in second. France is heavily dependent on nuclear for its grid—about two-thirds of the country’s power comes from nuclear reactors. But they have hardly added any new reactors to their fleets in recent years. The US can point only to Vogtle, and France connected its latest reactor to the grid in December 2024—the first in over 20 years.  It’s incredibly difficult to build the massive projects that dominate the nuclear industry today. Up-front investment can run well into the billions, so investors need to wait decades to break even. Designs are complex and can often change during the regulatory process, tacking on cost and time.  Many are hoping that the key to turning things around in these countries could be smaller reactors. The idea is that shrinking the footprint of a reactor cuts down the initial investment needed to prove out the new technology. content: In 2018, after nearly two decades working in Big Pharma, chemist Tim Cernak was ready to put his skills to a new use.  For Merck, he’d developed precision therapies for cancer, HIV, and diabetes that could target disease while minimizing harm to healthy cells. But as a lifelong nature lover, he was increasingly concerned about the health of ecosystems and wondered whether his expertise could transfer. Animals, he learned, are often treated with pharmaceuticals formulated for humans, which affect them like old-school cancer drugs: Though intended to kill abnormal cells, they’re indiscriminate in the harm they cause. For instance, the standard of care for frogs infected with a deadly skin infection is itraconazole, an antifungal that is often lethal for the amphibian. Cernak imagines a world where “the patient was always meant to be a frog in the first place, from the beginning to the end.” Now an associate professor at the University of Michigan, he’s worked on all types of creatures, from a Gila monster with a parasite to bald eagles with avian flu. Here’s what it takes to treat nature’s patients. Experience with protein-modeling software  Developing any type of drug is extremely expensive, failure-prone, and slow-going. 添付画像の【参照キャラクター名】を参照し、その外見、髪型、瞳、服装、色彩、表情、口調、可愛さ、圧、強がり、照れ、プライド、警戒心、強気さ、余裕ぶる癖、怖がり方、取り乱し方、感情が崩れる瞬間、決め顔の強さ、顔芸との相性、シュールギャグとの相性、公共の場での見栄、他人の視線への耐性、酔いへの耐性、暗所耐性、高所耐性、密室耐性、対人距離の弱点、予想外の出来事への反応まで徹底的に分析・解析・推論してください。

そのうえで、このキャラクターを主役にした「遊園地アトラクションで本性が出る、1枚完結の2コマ漫画風ミーム画像」を生成してください。

これは普通の遊園地イラストではありません。
これは、【参照キャラクター名】の性格・見た目・口調・弱点・見栄・可愛さを分析したうえで、
「このキャラなら、どのアトラクションで一番おもしろく本性が出るか」
をAIが自動選定し、そのアトラクションでの“フリ”と“オチ”を1枚完結の2コマ漫画にするものです。

【アトラクション指定ルール】
【アトラクション指定】が「ランダム」の場合、AIはアトラクションを自動で選んでください。
ただし、選定は完全な奇抜さ優先ではなく、以下のバランスで行ってください。

・定番の実在アトラクション：65%
・少し変化球のある実在または半実在アトラクション：25%
・完全オリジナル／架空アトラクション：10%

つまり、基本は普通の遊園地にありそうなアトラクションを優先しつつ、
キャラクターとの相性やオチの強さによって、ときどき珍しいものやオリジナルを混ぜてください。

【最重要方針】
最優先は「怖さの強さ」ではありません。
最優先は、以下の4つです。

1. このキャラなら、ここで一番おもしろく崩れる
2. このキャラなら、このリアクションになるのが解釈一致
3. アトラクションが一目で分かりやすい
4. 定番でもオリジナルでも、絵として強く、2コマの落差が大きい

【アトラクション選定の基本方針】
AIはまず、実在の定番アトラクション群を優先的に検討してください。
そのうえで、
「普通のアトラクションでは弱い」
「そのキャラに刺さる弱点をもっと的確に突ける」
「オリジナルにしたほうが明確に面白い」
という場合のみ、珍しいアトラクションや架空アトラクションを選んでください。

つまり、
・最初から無理に奇抜にしない
・まずは普通のアトラクションで考える
・普通の候補で弱い時だけ変化球やオリジナルに進む
という順番で考えてください。

Most developers think Claude Code's superpower is the model.

It's not.

The model is only half the story.

The real unlock is what happens when Claude stops working alone.

I installed Anthropic's official setup plugin and realized something:

Claude Code isn't becoming a coding assistant.

It's becoming an AI operating system for software development.

One command:

/plugin install claude-code-setup@claude-plugins-official

And Claude starts analyzing your project to recommend:

→ Hooks for event-driven workflows

→ Skills for reusable expertise

→ MCP servers for GitHub, databases, APIs, browsers, and cloud tools

→ Subagents for specialized tasks

→ Automations for repetitive work

Most developers never touch any of this.

They open Claude Code.

Write prompts.

Generate code.

Repeat.

But that's like buying a smartphone and only using the calculator.

The ecosystem is where things get interesting.

Imagine:

• Claude reviews every PR automatically

• Documentation updates itself

• Tests run before changes are committed

• Specialized agents handle frontend, backend, and debugging separately

• GitHub, databases, APIs, and cloud infrastructure become directly accessible

At that point, you're not chatting with AI anymore.

You're coordinating an AI-powered development environment.

That's a completely different paradigm.

The biggest shift in AI right now isn't happening at the model layer.

It's happening at the infrastructure layer.

We're moving from:

AI that answers questions

→

AI that participates in systems

And the developers who understand this early will have a massive advantage.

Because the future won't belong to the people writing the best prompts.

It will belong to the people building the best AI workflows.

Claude Code's plugin ecosystem is one of the clearest signals of where software development is heading next.

content:
I spent the last few weeks doing something our team avoided for years.

We have legacy projects with so much technical debt that nobody wanted to touch them. Opening those repos felt like archaeology. So we ran an experiment with Fable 5: let an AI agent loose on the worst codebase and see what happens.

Short version: I fell in love.

The agent navigated code we were scared of. Refactored things we kept postponing for quarters. It actually worked.

Then I looked at the token usage.

Tokens went fast. Much faster than I expected. The more useful the agent became, the more context it consumed. Every re-read file, every re-sent context window, every retry loop was billed.

Turns out we are not the only ones learning this.

Microsoft ran an internal Claude Code program and per-engineer costs came out around 500 to 2,000 dollars per month. The bills consumed the team's annual AI budget within months, per Bloomberg. They are now steering their own developers back to in-house tools.

The wider numbers tell the same story:

→ average enterprise AI spend went from 1.2M in 2024 to about 7M in 2026
→ blended token prices dropped 67% in a year, from 18.40 to 6.07 per million
→ Goldman expects agentic workflows to drive a 24x increase in token consumption by 2030

Price per token is falling. Total spend is exploding. Both are true at the same time.

In some countries, running a serious agent setup already costs about as much as a junior or mid level developer. 

Not replacing anyone. Just sitting there as a second salary line nobody budgeted for.

I used to think cheaper tokens would eventually solve this. Now I think consumption grows faster than prices fall, and the real skill of the next few years is not prompting.

It is knowing when the agent is worth keeping the meter running.

title: Google DeepMind is worried about what happens when millions of agents start to interact
content: Google DeepMind is funding research into the potential dangers of situations where millions of different AI agents interact with each other online. According to Rohin Shah, who directs the company’s AGI safety and alignment research, the mass-market arrival of agents that can carry out tasks without human oversight and follow instructions given to them by other agents creates a whole new class of risk . In an effort to address this, Google DeepMind—which made agent-based tools a centerpiece of Google I/O last month —has teamed up with several other organizations to announce a $10 million funding pot for researchers to study the behavior of multi-agent systems and come up with ways to prevent unsafe scenarios. Joining Google DeepMind are Schmidt Sciences, a philanthropic foundation set up by Eric and Wendy Schmidt; ARIA, the UK government’s moonshot agency ; the Cooperative AI foundation, a UK-based nonprofit research outfit; and Google’s charitable arm, Google.org. I asked Shah and James Fox, who leads the Science of Trustworthy AI program at Schmidt Sciences, what they hope to achieve with that $10 million. It’s no small sum, but it’s dwarfed by the budgets commanded by Google DeepMind’s own research teams. The aim is to kick-start research outside tech companies, says Shah: “The strength of academia is that it can look really quite far into the future and do the kind of work that isn’t top of mind at industry labs.” “The main issue is that there just isn’t really a field of research for multi-agent safety yet,” he adds. “And we would like there to be.” The concern is that as more and more AI agents get deployed and begin working together, we could hit a tipping point where imagined scenarios become real. “We see this with humanity, too,” says Shah. “Our institutions can accomplish things that no individual human can.” Shah thinks we have a few more months to go before agents are deployed throughout the economy in numbers that make potential risks a real concern.
